title: Reverse engineering a Viking VOIP phone protocol with Claude Code — Boris Starkov, Eleven Labs

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on Claude Code, a coding agent, autonomously performing reverse engineering tasks including port scanning, brute-forcing, protocol analysis, and packaging results as a reusable skill. Claude Code is a coding assistant applied to a novel cross-domain hardware reverse engineering task that does not fit a standard application vertical. The project describes a complete development cycle from initial exploration through implementation to open-source release. The content involves networking and reverse engineering concepts but is presented as an accessible conference narrative. Recorded conference talk with Q&A from AI Engineer Europe. summary: Boris Starkov, an engineer at ElevenLabs, recounts reverse engineering an undocumented Viking VoIP phone protocol using Claude Code over a couple of days. The Viking phone, purchased by ElevenLabs' San Francisco team a year prior, had defeated three senior engineers and ChatGPT because it required Windows XP-compatible software and nobody at the company had Windows laptops. Boris's goal was to connect the phone to an ElevenLabs conversational AI agent via Twilio, forming a chain: Viking phone, then Twilio, then ElevenLabs. Claude Code began by scanning the router network to find the phone, nmap-scanning its ports, finding port 1001 was an electronics tunnel, and then locating the correct communication port. It sent random sequences, received ER error responses, and deduced two-letter command codes. Claude Code brute-forced all 676 two-letter combinations, identifying 80 valid commands. Credentials could be written to temporary memory but were lost on reboot. A multi-hour effort to find a persistence command, including iterating all three-letter commands, reached a dead end—the same point where the original team had stalled. Claude Code then suggested running the proprietary Windows software in a Windows virtual machine and setting up a TCP proxy on the Mac to intercept traffic. Since Wi-Fi cannot be bridged to macOS in a VM, the proxy relayed communication while logging everything, revealing a previously unknown TS command with a binary payload containing a one-byte checksum. Claude Code reverse engineered the checksum formula through known input-output pairs, confirming it as a simple subtraction in a closed loop. With the protocol fully cracked, Boris packaged the knowledge as an open-sourced Claude Code skill, eliminating the need for the Windows software. Boris emphasizes he is not a security engineer and that Claude Code made the project possible, not just faster. He describes himself as Claude's hands—physically rebooting the phone and reporting beep counts while Claude orchestrated the intellectual work; he could not have unblocked the algorithmic parts himself. The physical setup used Power over Ethernet with a router between the phone and his laptop. Token cost was between $10 and $100 using corporate tokens. The outcome is a red phone booth demo at AI Engineer Europe where picking up the receiver connects to a Michael Caine voice agent quizzing visitors on British AI history.

sections.title: Introduction and demo overview
sections.summary: Boris introduces himself and describes the phone booth demo on the third floor where picking up the receiver connects to a Michael Caine voice agent that quizzes visitors on British AI history, with swag for answering at least one question correctly.

sections.title: Problem background and goal
sections.summary: The Viking phone only had Windows XP-compatible software, nobody at ElevenLabs had Windows laptops, and three senior engineers plus ChatGPT failed to configure it over a year ago. The goal is to connect the phone to an ElevenLabs AI agent via Twilio.

sections.title: Port scanning and protocol discovery
sections.summary: Claude Code nmap-scanned the phone's ports, found port 1001 was the wrong one (electronics tunnel), identified the correct communication port, and discovered the phone responds with ER errors to invalid commands, confirming an active protocol interface.

sections.title: Command brute-forcing and credential setup
sections.summary: Claude Code brute-forced all 676 two-letter command combinations, found 80 valid commands, and successfully wrote credentials to the phone's temporary memory, but settings were lost on reboot.

sections.title: Persistence problem and TCP proxy solution
sections.summary: After failing to find a persistence command via three-letter brute-forcing, Claude Code suggested a Windows VM with a TCP proxy on macOS to intercept the proprietary software's communication with the phone, revealing the unknown TS command with a binary payload.

sections.title: Checksum reverse engineering and open-source outcome
sections.summary: Claude Code reverse engineered the one-byte checksum through input-output pair analysis, confirmed it in a closed loop as a simple subtraction, cracked the 256-byte memory, and packaged everything as an open-sourced Claude Code skill. Boris emphasizes Claude Code made the project possible, not just faster, and the approach extends to other hardware.

sections.title: Q&A: token cost, role, and physical setup
sections.summary: In the Q&A, Boris reveals the token cost was between $10 and $100 using ElevenLabs corporate tokens. He describes himself as Claude's hands—following Claude's commands to physically reboot the phone and report beep counts—while Claude orchestrated all intellectual work. He could not have unblocked the algorithmic parts himself, only providing physical actions. The physical connection used Power over Ethernet with a router intermediary between the phone and his Wi-Fi-connected laptop. Claude's first step was scanning the router network to find all connected devices and locate the phone. The session closes with applause.
